dx: Hydropic villi of a complete mole

ww.Partial hydatidiform mole: Partial mole has two villous populations, swollen and normal-sized, with scalloped outlines and only focal trophoblastic hyperplasia. Here a rounded villus has a central cistern and a circumferential rim of proliferating trophoblast, which favors complete mole; p57 staining confirms it.
ww.Hydropic abortion (non-molar): Hydropic abortion has mildly swollen villi without circumferential trophoblastic proliferation, and the villi are usually smaller with scalloped or fibrotic stroma. A rim of proliferating, atypical trophoblast around a large swollen villus points to a mole.
ww.Choriocarcinoma: Choriocarcinoma is a sheet of malignant cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast with hemorrhage and necrosis, and it has no villi. This field shows an intact villus with a stromal cistern, so the trophoblast is growing on a villus, not as a villus-free tumor.
ww.Placental site trophoblastic tumor: Placental site trophoblastic tumor is a mass of monotonous intermediate trophoblast that infiltrates the myometrium between muscle fibers, with no villi. This section is built around a swollen villus, so it is molar tissue, not a solid tumor of intermediate trophoblast.

look: Look at the large villus in the center. Its core is pale, loose and nearly empty, a central acellular cistern formed by edema, and no blood vessels are visible in it. Along the upper and right rim, layers of trophoblast with larger, atypical nuclei form a circumferential collar, and a pool of blood lies at the left. Hydropic villi with circumferential trophoblast proliferation mark a complete mole.

findings: Hydropic villus: a large rounded villus with pale, loose, edematous stroma and a central acellular cistern sits at the center, swollen by fluid. This is the microscopic form of the grape-like vesicle seen on gross inspection.

Trophoblastic hyperplasia: along the upper and right border of the villus, layers of proliferating trophoblast with enlarged, atypical nuclei and vacuolated cytoplasm form a collar around it, reflecting paternal genes that drive trophoblast growth.
Absent fetal vessels: the swollen stroma is loose and nearly acellular with no visible capillaries, because the embryo failed to form and no fetal circulation supplies the villus.
Hemorrhage: a dense pool of red cells at the left edge, with fragments of villi, reflects the vaginal bleeding that brings most patients to care.
